brief.notification_title: AI bounce fizzles; Dell beats, PCE decides next
brief.market_summary: Monday's Nvidia-led rally reversed. The SOX fell 7.9%, SMH 7.3% and the Nasdaq 1.5%, while the S&P 500 lost 0.5% to 7,201. The Dow rose 0.85% as money moved into health care (XLV +2.95%) and staples (XLP +1.66%). Treasuries held after last week's rally: the 10Y was 4.904% (-1.4bp on the day, -19.9bp on the week) and the 5Y auction drew strong demand. Brent swung between a months-low $85.63 on hopes for US–Iran talks and a close near the day's highs on Hormuz attacks, with February settling at $88.78 (+$2.10). Bitcoin slipped back below $60K ($59,884) as spot ETF outflows set a monthly record.
brief.since_last: 1) The semis rebound failed. Nvidia fell about 6% as political backlash grew over Jensen Huang's reinstatement (n12, n26). ADI fell about 16% on guidance despite beating (single source). BNP cut Micron to Neutral, warning of oversupply (n3). 2) The WSJ reported tariff hikes on China, Japan, South Korea and more than a dozen others could come this week (n44). 3) The data split. Conference Board confidence jumped to 103.3 against about 92.3 expected (n79), but the S&P Global composite PMI missed at 54.6 vs 55.6 and the Chicago Fed index came in at -0.06 vs 0.20. 4) The Fed still leans hawkish. Williams won't rule out back-to-back hikes (n141), and most regional boards wanted a hike in October (n48). 5) After the close, Dell beat by a wide margin: EPS $9.45 vs about $6.61, revenue $54.9B vs $49.2B, and full-year guidance raised. The stock rose only 1.5–2.4% after hours, following a 13.3% fall in the regular session. 6) The Brent front month rolled. That's why the snapshot (-1.13%) and the settlement reports (+2.4%) disagree. 7) BTC is below $60K, with $2.37B of ETF outflows over five days.

Still expanding but slowing more than expected. It partly offsets the confidence beat and helped keep yields from rising.
A one-point miss. Manufacturing came in exactly at consensus (54.5 vs 55.6... see below), so services drove the miss. It's a mild growth-cooling signal, not a contraction.
In line with consensus, so no new signal.
Slightly below-trend activity, the second soft growth signal of the day. It's a minor release, but it adds to the case that Treasuries can hold their rally.
Housing is cooling under high mortgage rates. FHFA was flat at 0.0% vs +0.2% expected. This is disinflationary at the margin for shelter.
Cleared slightly below the last auction. Front-end demand is fine and nothing argues for a disorderly selloff in bonds.
The highest bid-to-cover since August, with indirect bidders taking 54.3%. Real-money demand for the belly backs staging into IEF.
Bill yields are still rising (the 6-month cleared at 4.340%), consistent with a Fed still hiking. SGOV's yield keeps improving.

This is the swing event. 0.4% or higher feeds Waller's 50bp December case and would push the 10Y back toward 5%; that cancels IEF tranche 2 and hits tech again. 0.2–0.3% lets the bond rally hold and could steady equities into the holiday.
An upward revision mostly confirms a strong economy and matters less than PCE, unless the price index surprises.

earnings.takeaway: A blowout, yet the stock rose only 1.5–2.4% after hours, to about $297–300, after falling 13.3% in the regular session to $290.50. AI demand isn't the problem; valuation and positioning are. That's not enough to lift semis by itself, so the SMH avoid holds until price confirms.

sections.summary: The cap-weighted indices fell because AI hardware sold off again: SMH -7.26%, XLK -3.26%, Nvidia about -6%, Micron about -10%, and Anthropic closed below its $83 IPO price. Underneath, the Dow (+0.85%), Russell 2000 (+0.57%), health care and staples all rose. That's a rotation, not a broad liquidation. Dell's large beat after the close drew only a small after-hours bid, so earnings strength isn't stopping the de-rating.
key_points: SMH closed at 426.75 (-21% over a month). Nasdaq-100 futures were -2.1% at 16:18 ET; I don't have post-Dell overnight quotes, so check live.
Nvidia is about 5% of the S&P (n69). Political risk is building: there's bipartisan backlash and Congress is moving toward China restrictions (n26).
Defensives are leading. XLV is +2.95% on the day and +3% over a month; Sanofi is buying Insmed for $41B (n15).
VIX is 26.4, up 43% over a month. Thanksgiving trading is thin, which amplifies moves either way.

sections.summary: Treasuries consolidated last week's roughly 20bp rally. The 10Y was 4.904% and the 5Y 4.712%, and strong 2Y and 5Y auctions show real demand as quant funds unwind bond shorts (n61). The front end is pinned by a Fed that is still hiking: 3-month bills cleared at 4.18%, above the 4.111% expected. Wednesday's core PCE decides whether the rally extends or gives back.
key_points: Par curve: 2Y 4.63%, 10Y 4.91%, 30Y 5.30%. 2s10s is +28bp; the 30Y barely rallied this week (-16.6bp vs -19.9bp for the 10Y), so term premium remains sticky.
5Y auction: 0.3bp tail vs a 0.9bp average, bid-to-cover 2.37 (highest since August), indirect bidders 54.3%.
Fed: Williams won't rule out back-to-back hikes (n141), Waller has floated 50bp, Bessent warns of over-tightening (n125). FOMC is 9 Dec, and the blackout starts Saturday.
Credit is softening slightly. HYG is -1.0% over a month and LQD -0.13% on the day, with no stress spike yet.

sections.summary: Brent has fallen about 24% in a month on hopes for US–Iran diplomacy and recovering supply. It hit $85.63 intraday on Tuesday, then closed near the highs after Iran's army chief ordered Hormuz kept closed and a tanker reportedly hit a mine. Price feeds disagree because the front month rolled on 23 Nov: February settled at $88.78 (+$2.10) per Newsquawk, the $91.40 in n23 likely refers to a different contract, and the snapshot's -1.13% is probably a roll artifact (BNO was +1.92%).
key_points: Bearish factors: Deutsche Bank estimates a 1.7 mb/d surplus, Saudi exports are recovering (n113), and Fujairah has resumed loadings (n129).
Bullish factors: Hormuz traffic is reportedly down 40%, and there are attacks on ships and talk of the US targeting Iran's leadership.
Goldman is reported as both cutting forecasts on a Hormuz reopening deal (n121) and raising its December call to $105. That conflict is unresolved, so don't lean on it.
OPEC+ meets online Sunday 29 Nov on 2027 baselines. Iraq wants about 6 mb/d recognised against a 4.431 mb/d quota (n91), and that dispute is a supply-discipline risk.

brief.instructor_take: Ignore the index print and look at how stocks reacted to their results. Dell doubled revenue and raised guidance, but only after falling 13% in the session. ADI beat and reportedly fell 16%, HPE gave back its gain after hours, and CrowdStrike fell 9% on a beat. When good news can't lift a stock, the multiple is being set by something other than earnings. Here that something is a Fed that is still hiking, with the 10Y near 4.9% and the 30Y at 5.3%. So I don't read Dell as the all-clear for AI. It tells me demand is fine and the valuations are the problem, and that resolves through price and time, not one report. The crowd may be missing that bonds have already done a lot: the 10Y fell 20bp in a week on safe-haven buying. A hot core PCE tomorrow (0.4% or more) would hurt both bonds and tech at once, and that's the scenario to respect. Consumer confidence at 103.3 tells me the economy isn't cracking, which keeps a December hike, possibly 50bp, live. My positioning stays a barbell: the cash core in bills earning about 4.2%, duration added in measured tranches only on in-line inflation, and no semis or crypto until price confirms, not narrative. Thanksgiving week liquidity is thin, so I'd make decisions on Wednesday's data and not chase Friday's half-session moves.

top_ideas.title: Keep T-bills as the core while the Fed hikes
top_ideas.one_liner: Bills yield ~4.2% and rising; SGOV funds every other move
top_ideas.thesis: The Fed is still hiking: Williams won't rule out back-to-back moves, and bill auctions keep clearing higher (3-month at 4.18% vs 4.111% expected). SGOV earns a rising yield with almost no price risk while equities and crypto de-rate. It's also the funding source for the IEF tranches and any later re-entry into semis.
top_ideas.reasoning: I start with the policy rate because everything else is priced off it. The 13-week yield rose to 4.168% from 4.143% yesterday, and Tuesday's bill auctions came in above expectations, so cash is paying more each week. Meanwhile the assets that usually compete with cash are struggling: SMH is down 21% in a month and BTC 26%, and even a blowout Dell report couldn't produce a real rally. This is the concept of opportunity cost turned around. When cash yields 4%+ and risk assets are being de-rated, the bar for leaving cash is high. I choose SGOV over SHY because SHY's 1–3 year duration takes a hit if PCE runs hot, while SGOV's doesn't. What a newer investor misses is that cash here is a position with optionality: it lets you buy SMH at 445 or BTC after a flush without selling something at a bad time. I'd change my mind if the 13-week yield broke below 4.0% or the Fed signalled December is the last hike. That would mean the market is pricing cuts and longer duration would do better.

top_ideas.entry: Keep the existing position. Sweep idle cash into SGOV at market on Wednesday. It's the funding source for IEF tranche 2 and any SMH or crypto rebuild.
top_ideas.invalidation: The 13-week yield (now 4.168%) falls below 4.0%, or Fed communication signals December is the final hike or a pause.
top_ideas.sizing: Hold as the portfolio's cash core, roughly 15–25%. Draw it down only to fund the defined triggers in ideas 2 and 3.

top_ideas.title: Stay out of semis until price confirms Dell
top_ideas.one_liner: Dell beat big but SMH is -7%; wait for 2 closes above 445
top_ideas.thesis: Semis are being de-rated despite strong fundamentals. ADI is down about 16% on guidance, Micron was downgraded on oversupply, Nvidia faces political and China-restriction risk, and tariffs are coming. Dell's beat drew only a small after-hours bounce. I need SMH to reclaim 445, about 4.3% above Tuesday's 426.75 close, before rebuilding.
top_ideas.reasoning: Yesterday's rule paid off: SMH fell 7.26% while we stayed out, even though Monday's gap looked tempting. Now I apply the concept of price confirmation over narrative. Dell's numbers ($9.45 vs $6.61 EPS, a $132B backlog) are as good as AI news gets, yet the stock is still below Monday's level and SMH closed at 426.75. That tells me sellers are using good news to exit, which is what a de-rating looks like. There are also several overhangs that earnings won't fix: Congress moving on Nvidia's China dealings (n26), a tariff announcement possibly this week, and a Fed that could hike 50bp on 9 Dec. A newer investor sees 'stock down 21% plus great earnings' and buys. I'd rather pay 4% more at 445 and know buyers are back in control. Two full-session closes above 445 end the avoid; Friday's half-day doesn't count. A close below 400 says the de-rating has another leg, and I'd extend the avoid past FOMC.

top_ideas.entry: No new semis buying on Wednesday, even if Dell lifts the open. Trigger: two consecutive full-session closes above 445 → buy half of the previously trimmed amount from SGOV. Buy the second half after a further week above 445.
top_ideas.invalidation: Two full-session closes above 445 end the avoid. A close below 400 extends it through the 9 Dec FOMC.
top_ideas.sizing: 0% new exposure. Any re-entry is half the trimmed amount (about 1.5–2% of the portfolio), then the rest.

top_ideas.title: Stage into 7-10Y Treasuries as an equity hedge
top_ideas.one_liner: Tranche 1 triggered at 4.90%; add tranche 2 only if PCE ≤0.3%
top_ideas.thesis: Strong 2Y and 5Y auctions, soft PMIs and the Chicago Fed miss, plus an equity de-rating, support the belly of the curve as a hedge. Tranche 1 triggered Tuesday with the 10Y at 4.904% after the 2Y auction. Tranche 2 depends on core PCE coming in at 0.3% m/m or lower.
top_ideas.reasoning: The reason to own IEF is the stock-bond hedge: if the AI de-rating spreads into a growth scare, 7–10 year yields fall and IEF rises while equities fall. Tuesday's evidence supports demand for duration. The 5Y auction had its best bid-to-cover since August with a tiny 0.3bp tail, and quant funds are unwinding bond shorts (n61). I pick IEF over TLT because the 30Y barely rallied (5.29%, and only -0.9bp over a month). The long end carries term-premium and fiscal risk, while the 5–10Y sector is where the move is happening. The tranche rule exists because inflation is the risk to this trade. Core PCE is expected to rise to 3.2% y/y and consumer confidence is strong, so a 0.4% print would make the Fed hike harder and push the 10Y back toward 5%. What I'm watching is whether bonds fall alongside stocks on a hot PCE print. If they do, the hedge isn't working and I keep it small. I'd be wrong if the 10Y closes above 5.15%, which costs about 1.7% on IEF.
catalysts: Wed 08:30 ET core PCE, GDP, jobless claims
risks: Core PCE at 0.4%+ or a hot GDP price index

top_ideas.entry: Tranche 1 (1.5%): triggered Tuesday with the 10Y at 4.904%; hold if filled near 91.64. Tranche 2 (1.5%): Wednesday after the 08:30 data, only if core PCE is 0.3% m/m or lower. top_ideas.invalidation: Core PCE at 0.4% m/m or higher cancels tranche 2 (hold tranche 1 under the stop). A 10Y close above 5.15% exits the whole position.
top_ideas.sizing: 3% total in two 1.5% tranches. Don't exceed that before FOMC.

lesson.concept: Beat-and-fade: expectations and positioning beat results
lesson.explanation: A stock price reflects the gap between results and what was already expected and owned, not the results alone. When a theme is crowded and the price has run up, a company can beat estimates and raise guidance and still fall, because the 'whisper' bar was higher and holders use the news to sell. When this happens across many companies at once, it usually means the market is lowering what it will pay for each dollar of earnings (de-rating), often because interest rates are high. The practical rule is to judge the reaction, not the headline: a strong report that can't produce a strong rally is a warning, not a buy signal.
lesson.todays_example: HPE beat by 16% and fell about 5% after hours. CrowdStrike beat and fell about 9%. ADI beat and reportedly fell about 16%. Dell beat EPS by roughly 43% ($9.45 vs $6.61) and rose only 1.5–2.4% after a 13% fall in the session. It's happening across companies, with the 10Y at 4.9% and the Fed still hiking. That's why the SMH re-entry depends on price (445), not on Dell's numbers.
